list.listitem: Suspect delayed gastric emptying when patients present with nausea, vomiting, early satiety, and abdominal pain, especially in the setting of diabetes, scleroderma, and neurologic disorders. C
After a mechanical obstruction is ruled out by endoscope or upper GI series, a gastric emptying scintigraphy study should be considered. C
Management consists of supportive measures and medications, including erythromycin, metoclopramide, cisapride, and domperidone (although evidence to support their efficacy is poor). B
Surgery, gastric pacing, and botulinum toxin are treatments of last resort that have limited or no evidence of efficacy. B

background.definition: Delayed gastric emptying or gastroparesis is a chronic motility disorder characterized by delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction.

list.listitem: Gastroparesis is more common in women (82% in one series of 146 patients at a referral center).
Gastroparesis is common in diabetic patients (40%-60%). However, only 5% to 12% present with symptoms requiring treatment.
Gastroparesis is also common among patients with nonulcer dyspepsia (24%-40% in several series).
Among patients with chronic small duct pancreatitis, one series found that 44% had gastroparesis.
Idiopathic (36%)
Diabetes (29%)
Postgastric surgery (13%)
Parkinson's disease (7%)
Connective tissue disorders - scleroderma, polymyositis (5%)
Chronic intestinal pseudoobstruction (4%)
Hypothyroidism
Renal failure
Medication induced - opiates, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers
Infiltrative disorders - lymphoma, amyloidosis
Miscellaneous - paraneoplastic, ischemic conditions, gastric ulcer, postinfectious (viral), brain stem lesions
Normal GI motor function is a complex sequence of events.

Gastric emptying is controlled by an extrinsic nerve supply from the brain and spinal cord, the complex plexi within the wall of stomach and intestine, and the effects of locally released transmitters such as amines and peptides that alter the excitability of the smooth muscle of the intestine.
Normal function involves slow waves at 3 cycles per minute in the stomach and 10 to 12 cycles per minute in the duodenum; normal meal emptying takes 90 to 120 minutes in a healthy individual.
The most frequent complaints are nausea (93%), abdominal pain (90%), early satiety (86%), and vomiting (68%). C
Exclude mechanical obstruction by upper GI series or endoscopy. C
The best initial study to confirm the presence of gastric stasis is scintigraphic gastric emptying. C

In a prospective series of 28 patients diagnosed with gastroparesis at a referral center, the most frequent complaints were nausea (93%), abdominal pain (89%), early satiety (86%), and vomiting (68%). The severity of symptoms correlates poorly with objective findings on scintigraphy.

The character of pain varies from burning to vague or crampy. The vomitus may contain old food ingested hours or days earlier. On examination, epigastric distention or tenderness may be noted but not guarding or rigidity. There may be presence of succussion splash.

The remainder of examination is aimed toward finding clues suggesting the presence of an underlying disorder resulting in gastric stasis (eg, findings of taut skin of hand and telangiectasia in scleroderma, delayed reflexes in hypothyroidism).
Exclude mechanical obstruction or mucosal disease with endoscopy or barium study. Consider a small bowel follow to exclude small bowel lesion in the presence of abdominal pain.

Consider hemoglobin, glucose, serum total protein, albumin, TSH, antinuclear antibody, and abdominal film to help assess nutritional status and determine degree of bowel obstruction. Also consider chest X ray in smokers with respiratory symptoms to screen for lung cancer as a cause of a paraneoplastic motility disorder. The actual clinical value of this evaluation is not known.

A gastric emptying scintigram using a radiolabeled solid meal is the recommended technique to confirm the presence of gastroparesis. Scans are taken immediately after a meal ingestion and 2 and 4 hours are usually enough for most clinical indications. Shorter protocols are not recommended. This approach was supported in a multicenter international study that established control values for normal gastric emptying.

As scintigraphy bears some radiation hazard, it may not be suitable for repeated investigations. An alternative nonradioactive study is the 13C-labeled octanoic acid or Spirulina algae breath test. However, this test has primarily been used in research studies and is not widely available. The MRI has also been used in research studies.

Gastroduodenal manometry can help differentiate a myopathic from a neuropathic etiology. Autonomic testing is useful in patients with neuropathic pattern to further determine the etiology. Other investigations (eg, cutaneous electrogastrogram and electronic barostat) are regarded as research tools with limited clinical applicability.
Suspect gastroparesis in the patient with nausea, early satiety, abdominal pain, or vomiting, particularly if they are diabetic or have a history of gastric surgery or neurologic disease.
Exclude mechanical obstruction or upper GI series. Endoscopy is more sensitive for detection of mucosal lesions.

Obtain a gastric emptying scintigram using a radiolabeled solid meal to confirm the diagnosis. Evaluation of the patient should include determination of the underlying cause (eg, diabetes, hypothyroidism).
Dietary modification (smaller, more frequent, low-fat meals) is commonly recommended. C

Prokinetics (eg, metoclopramide, erythromycin, domperidone, cisapride, and tegaserod) and antiemetics are the first-line medical therapy, but most studies have been relatively small, short, and of poor quality. B
Gastric stimulation and pacing does not appear to be effective, and surgery should be a treatment of last resort. B
Botulinum toxin injection into the pyloric sphincter is sometimes recommended but is invasive and has not been shown to be superior to placebo in 2 randomized trials. B

Both prokinetics (eg, metoclopramide, erythromycin, domperidone, cisapride, and tegaserod) and antiemetics (eg, prochlorperazine, trimethobenzamide, promethazine, and 5-HT3 antagonists) may be useful depending on the patient’s symptoms.

A systematic review of 35 clinical trials of erythromycin in patients with gastroparesis identified only 5 that gathered data on symptoms; all of these had 13 or fewer patients, were of short duration, and were poorly designed. Typical dose was 125 to 250 mg po tid. Evidence of effectiveness was mixed, and the best designed study (a double-blinded crossover trial) found no benefit.IV erythromycin is an option for patients who cannot tolerate oral medications (3 mg/kg IV every 8 hours).

Another systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 RCTs showed improvement in global symptoms scores only for clebopride (Clanzoflat, Cleboril), a chemical cousin of metoclopramide, and domperidone compared to placebo. Clebopride is not available in the US, while domperidone can only be used as an investigational drug in the US. A single small RCT (N=44) demonstrated metoclopramide had a small effect on nausea and bloating. Overall, there is lack of moderate- to high-certainty evidence for the efficacy pharmacotherapy for gastroparesis.

A systematic review identified 5 RCTs of metoclopramide for the treatment of gastroparesis, largely in diabetic patients using a dose of 10 mg 3 to 4 times daily. All but one found symptom improvement. Extra-pyramidal side effects and risk of tardive dyskinesia have reduced the use of this drug. Domperidone, not available in the United States, was shown in a small RCT to be similarly effective and to have fewer CNS side effects.

Cisapride stimulates 5HT(4) receptors, resulting in release of acetylcholine from the neurons in the myenteric plexus. The use of this drug in the United States is severely restricted (can only be filled by the manufacturer after providing documentation as to the need of drug and assessment of cardiac risk factors). Cisapride given 10 mg 3 times daily may reduce symptoms of gastroparesis compared with placebo, but it does not improve glycemic control in diabetics.
Newer prokinetic agents being tested include 5-HT4 receptor agonist tegaserod, the dopamine antagonist levosulpiride, and the cholecystokinin antagonist loxiglumide, but good data are lacking.

Surgery is a treatment of last resort for patients with nonobstructive gastric stasis. Completion or subtotal gastrectomy is an option for patients with previous partial gastrectomy.Percutaneously or laparoscopically placed gastrostomy or jejunostomy tubes are a treatment option for patients with chronic intestinal pseudoobstruction. None of these procedures has been well studied.
Gastric stimulation and electrical pacing has been studied in a few small trials, but no clinically important benefit was found.

Injection of botulinum toxin into the pyloric sphincter has been recommended based on several small uncontrolled case series that found 29% to 55% symptom reductions. However, a recent randomized double-blinded crossover trial found a similar benefit to botulinum toxin and a placebo in 23 patients. Thus there may be a considerable placebo effect with this intervention.
Similarly, a systematic review identified two randomized controlled trials of intrapyloric botulinum toxin that found no improvements in subjective symptoms compared to placebo.
Optimize glycemic control in patients with diabetes mellitus.
Dietary recommendations include a low-fat diet, small frequent meals, and avoidance of fiber, but clinical trials are lacking. The clinical benefit from dietary modification is thought to be modest.

In patients with more severe disease, a homogenized mixed meal or a liquid meal supplemented with vitamins may be helpful. If oral supplementation is unsuccessful, a jejunal feeding tube may be placed.
A Cochrane review found very low-certainty evidence to support acupuncture for short-term relief of diabetic gastroparesis. Randomized trials are small and of low quality.
A study of 20 diabetic patients with gastroparesis found no significant difference in measures of gastric emptying for solids or liquids after 12 years of follow-up. B
The same study also found no difference in symptom scores 12 years later. B
